Graph of Thoughts (GoT)

Generalizing reasoning topologies to arbitrary Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs), enabling complex transformations like aggregation and feedback loops.

Beyond Trees

While Tree of Thoughts allows branching, Graph of Thoughts (GoT) introduces the ability to merge branches. This is crucial for tasks that require synthesizing information from multiple distinct lines of reasoning. GoT models reasoning as a graph where vertices are thoughts and edges are dependencies.

graph LR Input[User Problem] --> A[Thought A] Input --> B[Thought B] Input --> C[Thought C] A -->|Refine| A1[Refined A] B -->|Refine| B1[Refined B] A1 & B1 & C -->|Aggregate| D[Synthesized Thought] D -->|Mutate| E[Final Solution] style Input fill:#0f172a,stroke:#38bdf8 style D fill:#1e293b,stroke:#818cf8,stroke-width:2px

Core Transformations

The GoT framework defines specific operations that the "Controller" (usually an LLM program) can perform on thoughts:

Generate (1:N)

Creating new independent thoughts from a single state (similar to branching in ToT).

Aggregate (N:1)

Combining multiple thoughts into a unified summary or conclusion. Unique to GoT vs ToT.

Refine (1:1)

Improving a single thought through self-correction or elaboration (Looping).

Network Architecture

GoT can be visualized as a modular network where prompts act as the processing engine for each node. Implementing GoT often requires a graph execution engine (like LangGraph) where the graph topology can be defined statically or dynamically.

Comparison

Method Topology Key Feature
CoT Linear Step-by-step continuity
ToT Tree Exploration & Backtracking
GoT Graph (DAG) Aggregation & flexible flow
